# Overview

Inverse-probability weighting (IPW) is the simplest of the
single-robust causal estimators. This vignette shows propensity-score
modelling, the Hajek-stabilised IPW estimator that
`morie_estimate_ate()` computes, the unnormalised Horvitz--Thompson
form for comparison, and weight diagnostics.

# Setting up

```{r setup}
library(rmorie)
set.seed(2026)
n <- 500
X1 <- rnorm(n)
X2 <- rnorm(n)
ps_true <- plogis(0.4 * X1 - 0.3 * X2)
treat   <- as.integer(ps_true > runif(n))
y       <- 1.0 * treat + 0.6 * X1 - 0.2 * X2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
df <- data.frame(y = y, treat = treat, X1 = X1, X2 = X2)
```

# Estimating propensities

`morie_estimate_ate()` fits a logistic propensity model internally and
returns the IPW estimate. To inspect or supply the propensities
yourself, fit them first and pass the column name as `propensity_col`:

```{r ps}
ps_fit <- glm(treat ~ X1 + X2, family = binomial(), data = df)
df$ps  <- predict(ps_fit, type = "response")
summary(df$ps)
```

# Hajek-stabilised IPW

`morie_estimate_ate()` computes the Hajek estimator, which divides
each weighted sum by the corresponding sum of weights. This
stabilises the estimator in finite samples when the propensity tails
are heavy. By default the propensities are trimmed to [0.01, 0.99]
(argument `trim`):

```{r hajek}
ate_hajek <- morie_estimate_ate(df, treatment = "treat", outcome = "y", covariates = c("X1", "X2"),
                          propensity_col = "ps")
ate_hajek$ate
ate_hajek$se
c(ate_hajek$ci_lower, ate_hajek$ci_upper)
```

The result is a list with `ate`, `se`, `ci_lower`, `ci_upper`, the
number of rows used and discarded by propensity trimming (`n_used`,
`n_discarded`), and the effective sample size of the weights (`ess`).

The Horvitz--Thompson form does not normalise the weights. It has no
separate function here; in base R it is:

```{r ht}
with(df, mean(treat * y / ps) - mean((1 - treat) * y / (1 - ps)))
```

On these simulated data the two forms are close. Hajek is the more
stable of the two when a few weights are large.

# Weight diagnostics

In practice, IPW is sensitive to extreme propensities. Two common
diagnostics:

```{r diag}
# ATE weights: 1 / ps for treated units, 1 / (1 - ps) for controls
w <- ifelse(df$treat == 1, 1 / df$ps, 1 / (1 - df$ps))

# Effective sample size after weighting
morie_effective_sample_size(w)

# Range of weights (extreme values suggest trimming)
range(w)
```

If the effective sample size collapses dramatically, the analysis
should consider:

- Trimming propensities to a sensible interval (e.g. [0.05, 0.95])
- Switching to a doubly-robust estimator (`morie_estimate_aipw()`)
- Adding more covariates to better separate the treatment groups

# AIPW for protection against IPW failure

```{r aipw}
aipw <- morie_estimate_aipw(df, treatment = "treat", outcome = "y", covariates = c("X1", "X2"))
aipw$ate
aipw$se
c(aipw$ci_lower, aipw$ci_upper)
```

When propensities are well-behaved, IPW and AIPW should agree to
within Monte Carlo noise. Disagreement is informative: it suggests
either model misspecification or a fragile propensity model.
